seoTitle: Livonia Personal Injury Attorney: How a Livonia Injury Claim Works, What It Is Worth, and What It Costs
seoDescription: Hurt in Livonia? How a Livonia injury claim works: the deadlines, the insurers, road agencies, and employers involved, the 16th District and Third Circuit courts, how damages are valued, and the one-third fee cap. ATLAW: 13 years, more than 10,000 cases. Free review. (313) 406-7606.
tagline: What a Livonia injury claim involves, from the first week to the check: the deadlines, the courts on Five Mile Road and in downtown Detroit, what the claim is worth, what it costs, and what to ask before you hire anyone.

c.v: If you were hurt in Livonia because someone else was careless, you have a claim under Michigan law, and its deadlines start the day you are hurt. After a crash, your no-fault insurer must have written notice within one year. A road or sidewalk defect claim against the City of Livonia or Wayne County needs written notice within 120 days; a defect on I-96, I-275, or M-14 needs written notice filed with the Court of Claims within 120 days. A claim against a bar that served a drunk driver must be filed within two years. A medical malpractice suit, including many claims against nursing homes, requires 182 days’ notice first and must be filed within two years. Most other claims allow three years. A personal injury lawyer’s first job is to find out which of those apply to you; the second is to make sure none runs out before your claim is paid.

ATLAW has practiced Michigan injury law for 13 years from its office at 3 Parklane Boulevard in Dearborn, has handled more than 10,000 cases, and has recovered more than $100 million for clients. Several injury firms have offices in Livonia, around Laurel Park and on Farmington Road among them. What matters more than an address is whether the lawyer knows the courts, the road agencies, the employers, the facilities, and the insurers your case will involve, and will meet you where you are. sections.heading: What a Livonia personal injury lawyer does

c.v: We calendar every deadline and send preservation letters:

items.v: to the at-fault driver’s insurer;
to a trucking company for its driver logs and electronic data;
to MDOT or Wayne County for signal timing records at the I-96 service drives and the mile-road intersections;
to SMART or the City for vehicle records;

to a store, a Laurel Park or Middlebelt property manager, an apartment or condominium association, or an employer on the Plymouth Road corridor for footage and incident reports, which many overwrite within days;
to a nursing home for the resident’s chart, incident reports, and staffing records;
to a bar for its receipts if a drunk driver was involved.

c.v: We obtain the police report (Livonia Police crash reports are available through CLEMIS; freeway crashes may be State Police reports), the Livonia Fire & Rescue EMS run sheet, and the witnesses’ names.

We identify every policy that may pay: your own auto policy for no-fault benefits, household policies, the at-fault party’s liability coverage, your uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage, a property owner’s commercial policy, umbrella policies, and the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan where no auto policy exists (MCL 500.3172). For a workplace injury, we identify whether a third party, such as a contractor, a vendor’s driver, or an equipment manufacturer, caused it, because the employer itself usually cannot be sued (MCL 418.131). We file your Application for No-Fault Benefits inside the one-year window (MCL 500.3145(1)) and handle the insurer’s requests for statements, records, and examinations (MCL 500.3151). You stop talking to adjusters; we do that.

The claim’s value is set mostly by the medical record, so we make sure it is complete and the bills are paid while you treat. We collect records from Trinity Health Livonia Hospital, Corewell Health Farmington Hills, Garden City Hospital, the Detroit trauma centers, and your own physicians and therapists, and document lost wages with your employer, including overtime and shift premiums.
The demand, the suit, and the resolution.

When your condition has stabilized, we send a demand with the complete record and a valuation. The decision to accept any offer is yours (MRPC 1.2). If the insurer will not pay fair value, suit is filed in the right court:

items.v: at 32765 Five Mile Road for claims up to $25,000, including mini tort claims.
at the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center in Detroit for injury suits over $25,000. The court may send injury cases to case evaluation (MCR 2.403) or facilitation before trial.
where the defendant lives or does business in Oakland County, or the injury happened on Eight Mile at the Farmington Hills line (MCL 600.1629).

c.v: At settlement we resolve the liens, including health plans, Medicare, Medicaid, and workers’ compensation, before you are paid. Minors’ settlements and wrongful death distributions are approved by the Wayne County Probate Court or the trial court (MCR 2.420; MCL 600.2922(6)). Compensation for physical injury is generally not taxable income (26 USC 104(a)(2)).

sections.heading: What a Livonia claim is worth, and what reduces it

c.v: A claim includes economic damages (medical expenses, lost wages, lost earning capacity, replacement services) and noneconomic damages (pain and suffering, loss of enjoyment of life, disfigurement). There is no cap except in medical malpractice. In an auto case, noneconomic damages require a threshold injury: death, serious impairment of body function, or permanent serious disfigurement (MCL 500.3135(1)). Your share of fault reduces the recovery, and above 50 percent it bars noneconomic damages (MCL 600.2959; in auto cases MCL 500.3135(2)(b)). At exactly 50 percent you recover half. Michigan does not award punitive damages in ordinary injury cases; exemplary damages for humiliation or outrage are available only in narrow circumstances.

In many Livonia cases the practical limit is insurance: the at-fault driver’s policy, often the $50,000 opt-down minimum (MCL 500.3009(5)); your own underinsured motorist coverage; and, in a premises, workplace, or nursing home case, the commercial policy of the property owner, contractor, or facility. Where UIM is involved, settling with the at-fault driver without your own insurer’s consent can forfeit the UIM claim. For a worker with a third-party claim, the workers’ compensation insurer has a lien on the recovery (MCL 418.827), and how that lien is negotiated changes what you take home.

Michigan caps contingency fees in injury cases at one-third of the net recovery (MCR 8.121). Case costs are advanced by the firm and deducted from the recovery first; the one-third fee is calculated on the remaining amount. You pay nothing up front and nothing if there is no recovery. The agreement is in writing; read how costs (filing fees, records, experts, depositions) are handled if the case is lost, because that is where firms differ.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in Livonia?

answer.v: Three years for most claims. But you have one year to notify your no-fault insurer after a crash, 120 days to notify the City or Wayne County of a defect, 120 days to file notice of a defect on a state road, two years to sue a bar, and a 182-day notice and two-year limit for malpractice.

faqs.question: What does a Livonia personal injury attorney charge?

answer.v: Michigan caps the fee in injury cases at one-third of the net recovery, with no fee if there is no recovery. Case costs are advanced by the firm and deducted only from a recovery.

faqs.question: Where would my Livonia case be filed?

answer.v: Claims up to $25,000 in the 16th District Court on Five Mile Road; injury suits over $25,000 in the Third Judicial Circuit Court in Detroit, or in some Eight Mile or Oakland County cases the Oakland County Circuit Court.

faqs.question: I was hurt at work in Livonia. Do I need a workers’ comp lawyer or an injury lawyer?

answer.v: Possibly both claims. Workers’ compensation pays your benefits regardless of fault, and your employer usually cannot be sued. If a contractor, a vendor’s driver, or a defective machine caused the injury, you also have an injury claim against that party, and the comp insurer is repaid from it.

faqs.question: If I was partly at fault, do I still have a claim?

answer.v: Yes, unless you were more than 50 percent at fault, which bars pain-and-suffering damages. Below that, your recovery is reduced by your share; at exactly 50 percent you recover half. No-fault benefits are paid regardless of fault.

faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer whose office is in Livonia?

answer.v: No. What matters is that the lawyer knows the courts your case will be in, the road agencies, employers, facilities, and insurers involved, and will meet you where you are.

faqs.question: How long will my case take?

answer.v: A no-fault benefits claim can resolve in months. A disputed injury claim in the Third Circuit often takes a year or two from filing.

faqs.question: The insurer already offered me money. Should I take it?

answer.v: Not before you know what the claim is worth and what the release gives up, and not before your UIM insurer has consented if UIM may apply.
